title: Chemistry 11 — Chapter 12: The Mixed Cylinder
description: A gas mixture cylinder needs its composition verified, and Friday's synthesis run needs the exact gas volumes calculated — molar volume, the ideal gas law, and Dalton's Law all come into play.

mika.name: Ms. Mika Tan
mika.description: Treats a gas cylinder like any other unlabeled sample — verify before you trust it.

dev.name: Dev
dev.description: Assumes all the gas laws collapse into one formula somehow.

molar_volume_card.name: Molar Volume Card
molar_volume_card.description: 22.4 L/mol at STP, and the ideal gas constant R.

mixture_readout.name: Mixture Pressure Readout
mixture_readout.description: Partial pressure data for each gas in the cylinder.

elements.text: Two jobs: verify what's actually in this mixed gas cylinder, and calculate exactly how much gas Friday's synthesis run needs.
Isn't it all just one big gas law formula at this point?

elements.prompt: Mika hands you the molar volume card.

options.text: "No — molar volume, the ideal gas law, and Dalton's Law each do a different job. Let's use the right one for each question."
"Pretty much, one formula should cover everything."

elements.text: Avogadro's Law: at the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes of any gas contain equal numbers of moles — the identity of the gas doesn't matter. At STP, that works out to a fixed molar volume: 22.4 L for one mole of any ideal gas.

config.question: Avogadro's Law states that at the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes of different gases contain:

options.text: Equal numbers of moles (particles), regardless of which gas it is
Equal masses, regardless of which gas it is
Equal densities
Different numbers of moles depending on the specific gas

config.explanation: Avogadro's Law is specifically about particle count, not mass or density — those still vary by gas identity.

config.prompt: At STP, molar volume is 22.4 L/mol. What volume (in L) does 2.00 mol of any ideal gas occupy?

elements.text: Molar volume only works at STP. Off those conditions, use the ideal gas law: PV = nRT, where R is the ideal gas constant, 8.31 kPa·L/(mol·K).

config.question: In the ideal gas law PV = nRT, what does R represent?

options.text: The ideal gas constant
The number of moles
A universal fixed temperature
The reaction rate

config.explanation: R is the ideal gas constant, 8.31 kPa·L/(mol·K) — it links pressure, volume, moles, and temperature together.

config.prompt: A sample is stored at 100 K in a 10.0 L container at 83.1 kPa. Using PV = nRT with R = 8.31 kPa·L/(mol·K), how many moles of gas are present?

elements.text: The cylinder's readout shows two different pressure numbers, one per gas. How do those combine?
Dalton's Law: in a mixture, the total pressure is just the sum of each gas's own partial pressure — as if each gas didn't notice the others were there.

config.question: Dalton's Law of partial pressures states that the total pressure of a gas mixture equals:

options.text: The sum of the partial pressures of each individual gas
The average of the partial pressures
The partial pressure of only the most abundant gas
The product of all the partial pressures multiplied together

config.explanation: Total pressure = sum of partial pressures — each gas contributes independently, as if the others weren't there.

config.prompt: The cylinder contains oxygen at a partial pressure of 60.0 kPa and nitrogen at 40.0 kPa, with nothing else present. What is the total pressure, in kPa?

elements.text: For Friday's run, combine what we already know: use the balanced equation's mole ratio, then molar volume at STP to convert moles of gas into litres.

config.question: When solving a gas stoichiometry problem, molar volume (22.4 L/mol at STP) is used to convert between:

options.text: Volume of gas and moles of gas
Mass and moles
Moles and molarity
Pressure and temperature directly

config.explanation: Molar volume is specifically the volume-to-moles conversion for gases at STP — mass uses molar mass, and molarity uses solution volume, not gas volume.

config.prompt: For 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, how many litres of O2 (at STP, 22.4 L/mol) are needed to fully react with 4.00 mol of H2? (mole ratio: 2 mol H2 per 1 mol O2)

elements.text: Composition verified, moles calculated, and Friday's gas volumes locked in. Every tool used correctly, for the right job.
We got through it, but a step or two needs another look. Let's revisit when to use molar volume versus the ideal gas law.

elements.prompt: The report is ready to close. What now?

options.text: Show Dev why molar volume, the ideal gas law, and Dalton's Law are three different tools, not one formula.
Close the report and move on. Good enough for today.

elements.text: So molar volume is the STP shortcut, the ideal gas law handles everything else, and Dalton's Law is just for mixtures. Three tools, three different jobs — not one formula trying to do everything.

ending.title: Gas Mixture Analyst
ending.description: Verified the cylinder's composition and calculated Friday's gas volumes using the right law for each step, correcting Dev's one-formula assumption.

ending.title: Report Closed
ending.description: The cylinder is verified and the run is calculated. The deeper tool-selection lesson can wait.
